rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to ensure all 6 compounds elute and reveal the full elution window and critical pairs. This should minimize truncation risk while giving useful retention and selectivity information for later optimization.

We are very close to the optimum, so now reduce gradient time one step while holding the same window and temperature to see whether all pairs remain above 1.5 and the last peak drops below 10 min. This directly tests the time-resolution tradeoff from the current best method.

Current conditions already achieve the maximum CRF, so the remaining value is to map the edge of failure and identify the shortest robust method. Reducing tG another step at the same window and temperature probes whether resolution stays acceptable under a still faster gradient.

At 4 minutes the worst pair is still just above the 1.5 threshold, so testing the minimum allowed gradient time will determine whether 4 minutes is truly the shortest fully resolving method or whether 2 minutes is still viable. This is the fastest way to locate the boundary and confirm the optimum.

Lowering temperature substantially improved the critical first pair at 4 minutes, so the key next test is whether that selectivity gain is enough to make the 2-minute gradient fully resolving. This is the most direct shot at finding a still faster maximum-CRF method.

The first pair improves as temperature drops, suggesting temperature—not gradient slope alone—is the best lever on this selectivity. Testing 40 C at the proven 4-minute method quantifies that trend and sets up the best chance of a successful 2-minute follow-up if the gain continues.
